The table you’ve supplied is drawn from the STAR2 manual’s front‐matter and Chapter 3 / Chapter 4 outlines. It is arranged as a three-column, hierarchical “Contents / Index” with the following key features:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Three top‐level entries (1 through 4), each representing one major chapter of the manual:  
     – 1 Task Description  
     – 2 Theoretical Principles  
     – 3 Input Description  
     – 4 Output Description  
   • A final “Bibliography” entry (unnumbered) at the end of Chapter 4.

2. Section Numbering and Indentation  
   • Main sections use integer labels (“1”, “2”, “3”, “4”).  
   • Subsections are denoted by “x.y” (e.g. “2.1”, “2.2” under Theoretical Principles; “3.1” through “3.11” under Input Description; “4.1” through “4.7” under Output Description).  
   • Deeper nesting is implied where sub‐subsections would be “x.y.z”, although not shown here.

3. Column Layout  
   • Left column: Section or subsection number.  
   • Middle column: Title or heading of that section (e.g. “Input Description”, “ECHO – Control of the Output Extent”, “Load Assembly”, etc.).  
   • Right column: Page reference, in “chapter–page” format (e.g. “3-31” means Chapter 3, page 31; “4-1” is Chapter 4, page 1).

4. Page Numbering Convention  
   • Chapter 1 uses Roman numerals (e.g. “i”).  
   • Chapters 2 and 3 use “2-x” or “3-x” to indicate chapter and page. In your excerpt, “3-31” is the start of the Input Description chapter.  
   • Chapter 4 pages run “4-1” to “4-7”.

5. Content of Chapters  
   – Chapter 1 (“Task Description”) briefly introduces the STAR2 family and its scope.  
   – Chapter 2 (“Theoretical Principles”) is split into seven parts (2.1 … 2.7), covering the mathematical background of 2nd/3rd order beam theory, shear deformation, material nonlinearities, etc.  
   – Chapter 3 (“Input Description”) enumerates eleven subsections (3.1 … 3.11) where each 3.x describes one input card or group of cards that the user must supply to define geometry, materials, loads, supports, prestress, eccentricities, creep, and so forth.  
   – Chapter 4 (“Output Description”) contains seven parts, each documenting one type of output:  
     • 4.1 Load Assembly  
     • 4.2 Output of the Structure  
     • 4.3 Results  
     • 4.4 Output during Iterations  
     • 4.5 Convergence Criteria  
     • 4.6 Design Output  
     • 4.7 Stiffness Computation  
   – After Chapter 4, the “Bibliography” appears on page 4-7.

6. Formatting Details  
   • Dot‐leader lines connect titles to their page numbers for quick scanning.  
   • Uniform indentation signals the hierarchy, making it easy to see which subsections belong to which chapter.  
   • The consistent three-field layout (number / title / page) is repeated for both the input and output tables.

How this maps to a RAG‐style vector store  
– Each numbered subsection (e.g. “3.5 Cross-Section Definitions” if that were the actual title) can be treated as a distinct document or vector embedding entry.  
– The “chapter–page” notation provides a stable, human‐readable reference link back into the manual PDF.  
– The parent–child relationships (chapters → subsections) allow you to build a hierarchical index, enable drill-down queries (“Show me all input cards related to prestressing”) or broad queries (“What inputs are needed to control material nonlinearities?”).

4-3. 4-4. Bibliography. 4-7. 1 Task Description. The programs of the STAR-family enable the computation of the internal forces in any three- dimensional beam structure by 2nd or 3rd order theory taking into consideration shear defor- mations as well as various non-linear material effects..
 STAR1 - 3D version without design
 STAR2 - 2D version with design
 STAR3 - 3D version with design
 Effects of 3rd order theory are available for truss and cable elements.
 The static system must be described by the user in terms of discrete elements, and the corre- sponding database must be defined by the generation program.
 Available elements are:
 • Beam element with straight axis and step-by-step constant arbitrary cross section. Analysis by 2nd order theory with consideration of the shear deformation. Consideration of non- linear material behaviour through iteration.
 • Spring element such as support spring or node-coupling spring; non-linear effects include slip, failure, yielding and friction.
 • Truss element with prestress
 • Cable element with prestress (only tensile force is possible)
 • Distributed support element for elastic support of beams
 • Couplings for special effects like eccentric beam links, rigid links between nodes etc.
 Disk or plate elements as well as solid elements, which can be defined by the generation program, can not be processed by STAR2. The foundation definitions for pile elements are not available in STAR2 either.
 Concentrated forces or moments may act on the nodes, while support translations or rotations can be defined at any support. The beam elements can be loaded with point loads at any po- sition in the form of eccentrically acting forces, moments, jumps in displacement or rotation, as well as with linearly varying loads in the form of forces, moments, strains, curvatures or temper- ature strains. Unintentional eccentricities of linear, quadratic or cubic variation can be defined for the analysis with 2nd order theory. In addition, creep deformations or unintentional eccen- tricities can be generated from already analysed load cases. Prestress can be considered by specifying an MV0 or NV0 distribution.
 The analysis of frames by 2nd order theory with consideration of material behaviour is a de- manding engineering task. The user of STAR2 should therefore accumulate experience from simple examples, before attempting to take on more complicated structures. A check of the results by off-hand engineering calculations is indispensable.

The static problem is solved by the deformation method. In any iterative technique, non-linear properties must be decomposed into several individual linear steps by an iterative method. A closed form solution can be computed by 2nd order theory for such a linear step, if the stiffness and the axial force are assumed constant.

The program uses exclusively right-handed coordinate systems in accordance to DIN 1080 for the description of force-, moment-, displacement- or rotation-vectors. The three-dimensional global system of coordinates serves in defining the nodal coordinates and displacements or rotations.
 Each beam gets a local coordinate system, which is defined by the generation program. Beam deformations and internal forces and moments are output in this coordinate system. When confusion is possible, the local xyz-system is also designated by S12.
 Thus, the essential magnitudes for primary bending are:
 Cross section values AZ, IY Forces, displacements, moments Z or 2 Rotations, curvatures Y or 1 Internal forces and moments
 VZ, MY
 and for secondary bending:
 Cross section values AY, IZ Forces, displacements, moments Y or 1 Rotations, curvatures Z or 2 Internal forces and moments
 VY, MZ
 Internal forces and moments are positive if they act in the positive directions of the axes at an end cross section (when moving in the longitudinal direction of the beam).

The illustration presents a single, straight beam segment in free-body view, annotated with both global and local coordinate systems and the principal internal forces and moments that act on an arbitrary cross section. Key features and annotations are as follows:

1. Beam Geometry and Cross Section  
   • A prismatic beam element is drawn in three-dimensional isometric projection. Its axis is a straight line running from the “near” face (where the cross section is hatched) back to the “far” end of the beam.  
   • The right-most end face is hatched at a 45° angle, indicating the location of the cut section under consideration. A second, smaller rectangular cross section is shown just behind the hatched face, emphasizing the local coordinate origin at that section.

2. Global Coordinate System (X, Y, Z)  
   • In the lower-left corner, a triad of orthogonal arrows—labeled X (horizontal, pointing right), Y (horizontal, pointing away from the viewer), and Z (vertical, pointing upward)—defines the global, fixed reference frame in which all beam segments are embedded.  

3. Local (Section) Coordinate System (X′, Y′, Z′)  
   • At the hatched cross section, a second triad is drawn: X′ runs along the longitudinal axis of the beam pointing toward the right end; Y′ points into the page (or into the section) at an angle consistent with the beam’s orientation; Z′ is vertical, pointing downward in the view.  
   • This local frame coincides with the beam’s neutral axis (X′) and its principal bending axes (Y′ and Z′), averaged over the segment according to the reduction method (transfer-matrix approach) under the assumption of constant axial force per segment.

4. Internal Forces and Moments at the Cut Section  
   • Axial Force (Nₓ): Illustrated by a downward arrow aligned with the local X′-axis, denoting tensile or compressive loading along the beam axis.  
   • Shear Forces: Qᵧ is shown as an arrow approximately parallel to the local Y′-axis (into the page), and Q_z is depicted along the local Z′-axis (vertical).  
   • Bending Moments: Mᵧ is drawn about the local Y′-axis (an arrow curving around the section in a plane normal to Y′), and M_z about the local Z′-axis (curving around Z′).

5. Interpretation in Context of the Text  
   • The beam is treated as a straight element whose stiffnesses and axial force are “averaged” over its ends, satisfying the assumptions of second-order theory (small rotations, unchanged orientation of axes).  
   • No warping of the cross section or 3rd-order large‐deformation effects are shown, consistent with the implementation notes indicating only 2nd-order torsion and shear deformations are available.  
   • The depiction underscores how any offset between the shear center and the centroid can be accommodated by a rotation of the principal axes with respect to the global frame.

Together, these details form a comprehensive free-body diagram of a beam element used in advanced structural analysis via the reduction (transfer-matrix) method, clarifying both geometry and internal loadings in global and local coordinates.

The individual beam elements are analysed by the reduction method (method of transfer ma- trices) under the assumption of step-by-step constant axial force. The following assumptions are made as well:
 The beam axis is a straight line. Broken or curved beams must be replaced by several straight beam segments. The beam axis coincides with the neutral axis. The stiffnesses and the axial force for each particular segment are averaged from their end values. Therefore, in case of highly varying values, one should be careful to define a sufficient number of segments (usually
 5 to 10).
 The theory of 2nd order satisfies the equilibrium conditions for the deformed structure. The ori- entation of the beam axes (transverse force instead of shear force) and the forces (conservative loading) remain unaltered. By contrast, the theory of 3rd order considers large deformations, which alter the orientation of the local system of coordinates. The 3rd order theory is not yet implemented for beam elements. Thus, by 3rd order theory all beam elements are handled in the same ways as by 2nd order theory.
 For frame design without use of the effective length factor, the term advanced analysis refers to second-order inelastic analysis [10] .
 The stiffnesses can be modified due to the material by design only (input record NSTR). They remain constant within an iteration step, whereas without NSTR they remain constant during the entire analysis.
 Torsion according to St. Venant (no lateral warping of the cross section). Warping and torsion according to theory of 2nd order are not implemented in STAR2.
 The effect of shear deformations due to shear force can be taken into consideration.
 A deviation between the shear centres and the centre of gravity can be ultimately considered as a rotation of the principal axes with respect to the system of coordinates of the beam.

The separate analysis in the primary and secondary direction is correct only when the axes y and z are the principal axes of the cross section. If this condition is not satisfied, the deforma- tions are not computed correctly in case of statically determinate structures, whereas in case of statically indeterminate structures the internal forces and moments are wrong too. STAR2 transforms all the loads and the internal forces of three- dimensional structures into the direc- tions of the principal axes. Variable rotation along the length of a beam can not be considered however. This transformation can be suppressed in special cases. The principal axes are
 always taken into consideration correctly during design, when biaxial bending is active.

The image consists of three side-by-side schematic force–displacement diagrams, each plotted with force P on the vertical axis (positive upward) and displacement V on the horizontal axis (positive to the right). A light dotted vertical line marks the zero‐displacement origin in all three plots; likewise, a light dotted horizontal line marks zero force. Each diagram illustrates one of the non-linear spring effects discussed in the adjoining text. Directly beneath the three plots is the caption “Figure 2.2: Force-displacement diagrams of springs.”

1. Leftmost diagram (GAP behavior)  
   • The horizontal axis is labeled “V”; the vertical axis is labeled “P.”  
   • Near the origin, the spring exerts no force for small displacements: the force curve is flat (zero force) between two symmetric displacement thresholds. On the positive side, a bracket with arrows marks the distance from zero displacement to the point where force first becomes nonzero; this bracket is labeled “GAP.” An identical bracket appears below the axis on the negative-displacement side, also labeled “GAP.”  
   • Once the displacement exceeds the positive gap threshold, the curve rises linearly with a constant positive slope (representing the spring’s stiffness). Likewise, once the displacement exceeds the negative gap threshold in the negative direction, the curve drops linearly with an equal but opposite negative slope.  
   • This model captures a “dead” zone (free play) of width 2·GAP in which the spring carries no load, followed by linear elastic response.

2. Center diagram (CRACK behavior)  
   • Again, axes P (vertical) and V (horizontal) are shown, with the origin marked.  
   • In the negative‐displacement region (to the left of the origin), the force–displacement relationship is linear with a relatively stiff slope. Along the left vertical projection of the origin, a short horizontal tic marks zero displacement, and just to its left a small bracket labeled “CRACK” indicates that upon unloading or compressive movement the spring no longer sustains tension beyond a certain small opening.  
   • In the positive‐displacement region (to the right of zero), the line from the origin has a shallower slope than in compression. At some prescribed positive displacement, the slope abruptly increases again to the original stiffer value. In other words, the crack‐mode spring shows reduced stiffness in a certain opening range, then re-engages full stiffness beyond that opening.

3. Rightmost diagram (+YIELD– behavior)  
   • The axes are the same P–V pair, origin indicated.  
   • In the compression (negative V) region, the spring exhibits linear elastic response with a single constant slope down to some negative yield displacement. No special labeling appears on the negative side, but the transition is implicitly analogous to the positive side.  
   • On the positive side, the curve rises linearly from the origin with the initial stiffness until it reaches a displacement marked by a short horizontal bracket on the V axis labeled “+YIELD–”. At that yield threshold the force plateaus: the curve becomes horizontal, indicating that further displacement occurs at essentially constant force. Beyond some larger displacement not explicitly marked, the curve then resumes an upward incline (a second, stiffer elastic region), although the schematic only hints at this by a slight angled line beyond the plateau.  
   • This plot models idealized yield behavior: elastic up to a limit, plastic slip at constant force, then strain hardening upon further displacement.

Overall, the three sketches illustrate non-linear spring characteristics—free-play gaps, crack‐opening softening, and yield/plasticity—each plotted in the same P–V coordinate frame and serving as visual supplements to the text’s description of how prestress, failure, yield, friction, cohesion, and slip can be incorporated into spring elements during non-linear structural analysis.

The input figure is composed of two adjacent P–v diagrams, labeled “Figure 2.3: Iteration methods a / b,” illustrating the two nonlinear‐analysis iteration schemes described in the accompanying text. In both diagrams, the vertical axis represents load P (force), and the horizontal axis represents deformation or displacement v. Each subfigure shows:

1) A bilinear (or more generally nonlinear) “spring” response curve—drawn in a solid, relatively thick line—that departs from the origin with an initial stiffness E₀ (the slope of the first segment), transitions at a yield or softening point, and thereafter follows a lower tangent (a horizontal plateau in the left figure and a less steep segment in the right figure).

2) A horizontal dashed line, at a P‐level above the initial elastic plateau, indicating either the target force (in stress control) or the previous‐iteration force level used to define a secant stiffness.

3) A dashed line drawn from the origin to the intersection of the prescribed displacement or force with the nonlinear response curve. That line represents the secant stiffness Eₛ computed at the current iteration.

Detailed walk-through of each subfigure:

Left: Method a – Strain Control  
- The nonlinear P–v curve starts at the origin with straight slope E₀ (the initial elastic modulus).  
- At a certain displacement (marked by a vertical dashed line dropped down to the v‐axis), the curve levels off into a flat plateau, indicating yield or softening (constant P).  
- A vertical dashed line at that displacement shows the prescribed v for this iteration.  
- Where that vertical line meets the nonlinear curve, a point is marked. From that point, a dashed line is drawn horizontally out to the P‐axis—identifying the computed force for the given v—and back to the origin, forming the secant line whose slope is Eₛ.  
- The horizontal dashed line at the level of that computed P is shown extending across the plot, emphasizing the force value obtained.

Right: Method b – Stress Control  
- The same basic bilinear response is shown: initial slope E₀ up to yield, then a shallower, approximately horizontal segment.  
- Here, a horizontal dashed line indicates the prescribed force P for the iteration.  
- Where this horizontal line intersects the nonlinear curve, a point is marked. From that intersection, a dashed line is drawn down to the displacement axis to show the computed v corresponding to the applied P.  
- A dashed line from the origin to this intersection point again defines the secant stiffness Eₛ for the current iteration.  

Below the two plots is the caption “Figure 2.3: Iteration methods a / b.” The left diagram is understood to use method a (strain control—prescribed displacement, solve for force, then update secant stiffness), while the right uses method b (stress control—prescribed force, solve for displacement, then update secant stiffness). Together, the pair visually contrasts how secant stiffnesses are derived in each control scheme during a nonlinear structural‐analysis iteration.

Spring elements model structural parts by a simplified force- displacement relationship. This is usually expressed by means of a spring constant in the form of a linear equation:
 P = c ·
 (2.18)
 The spring is defined by its direction ( DX, DY, DZ ) and the spring constants. The direction can be determined as the difference of two nodes (N2 - NA), or it can be specified explicitly. Support springs must be provided with a direction (see generation program). The element implemented herein allows for the following non-linear effects:
 - Prestress (linear effect)
 - Failure
 - Yield
 - Friction with cohesion
 - Slip
 Geometrically non-linear effects are not possible for springs.
 A prestress shifts the corresponding effects and it always generates a loading upon the struc- ture. A prestressed spring is relaxed in the absence of external loading or compulsion. The non-linear effects apply to rotational springs as well as lateral springs too. Friction can be defined by a lateral spring. The force components normal to the spring’s direction of action are equal to the product of the displacement components in the lateral direction by the lateral spring constants. This force is at most equal to the product of the force in the normal direction by the friction coefficient plus the cohesion. If the normally oriented spring is eliminated, the lateral spring is automatically eliminated too.
 All spring non-linearities are activated only during a non-linear analysis. To this end, a value for the number of iterations must be specified by the analysis methods in CTRL.
 Upon such request (see input record CTRL) either the force corresponding to a prescribed displacement value will be determined within an iteration (strain control a) or the displacement for a prescribed force (stress control b). A secant stiffness results from the values computed in this way. Method a should be used by structures, which soften as they are loaded, whereas
 method b should be used for stiffening structural members.
 The user must take care so that the system does not become unstable in any step of the iteration through failure of springs or cables. This can happen, for instance,if one defines additional springs with small stiffness, resulting to a small remaining stiffness after the main spring’s failure. This stiffness should not be less than the stiffness of the main spring divided by 10000.

Trusses can be analysed by 2nd or 3rd order theory. 2nd order theory is considered as de- scribed in /9/; nodal deformations are additionally taken into account in the construction of the element matrices by 3rd order theory.

Cable elements are handled similarly to trusses. Cables can not sustain any compressive forces. 2nd and 3rd order theories are applicable as for trusses. A correct computation is generally possible through several iterations only.
 In order to analyse a cable structure, which is usually stable only under loading, by 1st order theory too, it is assumed that the elements are subjected to a small prestress.

A global stiffness matrix is obtained by adding all the individual element stiffnesses; after in- corporating the geometric boundary conditions, the displacements and thus the internal forces get computed. If non-linear springs or a redistribution of the axial force are present, the input of a number of iterations within the defined limits will force the whole process to be repeated by updating the secant stiffnesses until a solution is obtained.

The number of load cases is limited to 999.
 The number of nodes, beams, sections or loads is only limited by the amount of the available disk space. 5 digits are usually reserved for the output of their numbers, thus values above
 99999 should not be used.
 STAR2 works with double precision. Despite that the following points should be considered:
 1. The stiffness EI/l3 of neighbouring beam elements may not differ by a factor larger
 than 10-5.
 2. Beam theory is valid only for structural members, the length of which is at least twice their height. The length of each individual element should not be smaller than the height of the cross section used.
 3. Artificially rigid elements can and must be defined as couplings.
 If these criteria are not met, reaction forces will arise on free nodes.
 STAR2 sets a constant stiffness for each segment. The buckling length coefficient β after Pe- tersen /6/ p.489 reaches a maximum of 1.22 for a conical beam under its own weight compared to 1.12 for a prismatic beam (8% error). If the dimensions are changed by just 10% (I-Value by 27.1%), β reaches 1.14, corresponding to an error of about 2%.

Initial deformations (unintentional eccentricities) are deviations of the actual beam axis from the ideal beam axis. These are independent of self-arising deformations. They have no effect on an analysis by 1st order theory.
 The following variations are possible:
 Linear inclination (e.g. DIN 1045 Sec. 15.8.2)
 Input in the form of a point load at the column head.
 Arbitrary step-by-step linear variation.
 Input in the form of distributed load.
 Arbitrary shape related to the buckling mode (e.g. DIN 1045 17.4). Defined either by several positions along the column, connected by a cubic spline, or by the bending line from an already analysed load case.

DIN 1045 requires an estimation of the effects of creep and shrinkage according to Section 17.4, when the slenderness of the compressed member is greater than 70 for immovable or 45 for movable structures and at the same time the eccentricity e/d is smaller than 2.
 Creep deformations are computed for the permanent loads acting in the service state as well as for any prescribed permanent beam deflections and eccentricities including the unintentional ones.
 An approximate method using an increased unintentional eccentricity is described in note 220 of DAfSt.
 STAR2, however, can perform a more accurate check. A load case is built for this purpose from the loads that cause creep. The resulting deformations, multiplied by a creep factor, can be
 used either as initial deformations or as curvature loads during a subsequent run. The same method allows the consideration of construction phases.

A fixed prestress can be specified in the generation program for springs and trusses. This acts by every load case and generates corresponding stresses. A prestress for each individual load case can be defined in STAR2 as well.
 A statically determinate component of the prestress (NV0,MV0) for each load case can be defined separately for bending beams. Then, depending on the number of parameters, any variation of these values from constant to cubic can be assumed along the beam axis. The effect of prestress is twofold. On one hand, the internal forces and moments are modified by the corresponding prestress values, and on the other hand, deformations result from prestress, which in turn lead to compulsory forces in cases of statically indeterminate structures.
 Prestress is considered differently for cables and for beam elements. A cable or a truss can be only prestressed through the external system. Therefore, the prestress is then analysed like a temperature stressing caused by a strain imposed on the element. Forces are generated within the elements of an undeformed structure, whereas in deformed structures the prestress deteriorates due to self-arising deformations. If one wants to receive a defined prestress, one must employ therefore an element with very small strain stiffness.
 For beams, by contrast, prestress is defined as an independent state of stress (prestressed concrete). Since the prestress is imposed on the element itself, the resulting forces on freely deformable beams are the input internal forces themselves. If the deformation is hindered, compulsory forces arise. In the limiting case, e.g. if a beam is prevented from deforming in the longitudinal direction, the resulting axial force is null, because the forces imposed by the prestressing steel are resisted by the support instead of the beam.

The shear deformation can be also taken into account by the beam elements. The program AQUA defines the standard shear areas for some cross sections. The internal force variation in statically indeterminate structures may differ from the one obtained by pure bending theory, if shear deformation is taken into consideration.

Since the design or stiffness computation by AQB must be activated for an iteration with non- linear material behaviour after any static analysis, the most important records of AQB are also available in STAR2. These are:
 CTRL - General parameter
 REIN
 - Special parameter for DESI and NSTR
 DESI - Reinforcement computation
 NSTR
 - Strain state
 The complete theory for these records can be found in the AQB manual. Only the descriptions of the input records are given in this manual.
 If not all of the beams are to be dimensioned in the same way, this can be avoided by an external iteration via the record processor PS.

The input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUC- TURAL Installation and Basics’). Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table is a compact summary of all the “records” (input‐line identifiers) understood by the program and, for each record, the list of positional or keyword “items” that may follow.  In practice the user feeds one or more blocks—terminated by ENDE—and within each block uses these records to define loads, analysis parameters, groupings, design checks and so on.  Below is an annotated walk‐through of each record line in the table:

1. ECHO  
   • Items: OPT, VAL, SELE  
   • Purpose: Controls echoing of input data to the listing.  OPT switches echo on/off, VAL can limit which records are echoed, and SELE further refines the selection.

2. CTRL  
   • Items: OPT, VAL  
   • Purpose: Switches between generation‐only, analysis, or restart runs and selects analysis order (1st, 2nd, or 3rd order), iteration limits, axial‐fix strategies, cable behavior (CABL vs. TRUS), group divisors, and references to primary load cases for linearized second‐order stiffness.

3. GRP  
   • Items: NO, VAL, STIF, SECT, SC, PRES, FACS, FACG, CS, FACP  
   • Purpose: Defines element or node groups for stiffness, section assignments, prestress values, factor sets and group‐specific control parameters.

4. INFL  
   • Items: NO, TITL  
   • Purpose: Introduces an “influence line” definition.  NO is the identifier, TITL is an optional title.

5. LC (Load Case)  
   • Items: NO, FACT, DLX, DLY, DLZ, TITL, TYPE, GAMU, GAMF, PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S, GAMA, CRI1, CRI2, CRI3  
   • Purpose: Defines a single load case.  NO is the load‐case number; FACT is a global scale factor; DLX/DLY/DLZ are offsets; TYPE selects load‐case type (e.g. dead, live, wind); GAMU/GAMF are partial factors for ultimate/serviceability; PSI0–PS2, PS1S, GAMA are combination factors per EN 1990; CRI1–3 reserve up to three user‐defined criteria flags.

6. LCC (Load‐Case Combination)  
   • Items: NO, FACT, FROM, TO, INC, NFRO, NTO, NINC, TFRO, TTO, TINC, CFRO, CTO, CINC  
   • Purpose: Builds envelope or combination of several load cases.  You can specify ranges (FROM–TO, INC) for cases and for factors (NFRO–NINC), temperatures (TFRO–TINC), or combination factors (CFRO–CINC).

7. LV (Load Variation)  
   • Items: NO, PHI, EPS, FACV, FROM, TO, INC, STIF, CSMI, CSMA, KTYPr  
   • Purpose: Parameterizes continuous variation of loads or actions (wind direction, moving loads, etc.).  PHI and EPS define the variation law; FACV is a scale; STIF or CSMI/CSMA allow stiffness updates along the path; KTYPr picks the variation type.

8. *REIN (Reinforcement Control)  
   • Items: MOD, RMOD, LCR, ZGRP, SFAC, P6–P12, TITL  
   • Purpose: Switches on design checks for reinforcement or steel sections: selects modules (zone‐by‐zone or global), load‐case references, partial safety factors, up to seven user parameters P6–P12, and an optional title.

9. *DESI (Design/Stiffness Computation)  
   • Items: STAT, KSV, KSB, AM1–AM4, AMAX, SC1–SC2, SS1–SS2, C1–C2, S1–S2, Z1–Z2, SMOD, TVS, MSCD, KTAU, TTOL, TANA, TANB, SCL  
   • Purpose: From AQB, controls detailed design and stiffness‐update options: selection of bending types, activation of nonlinear strain effects, iteration parameters, rounding rules, shear‐force conversion, cover requirements, envelope generation strategy, and tolerances.

10. *NSTR (Nonlinear Stress/Strain)  
   • Items: KMOD, KSV, KSB, KMIN, KMAX, ALPH, FMAX, SIGS, CRAC, CW, BB, HMIN, HMAX, CW‐, CHKC, CHKT, CHKS, FAT, SIGS, TANS, TANC  
   • Purpose: Also from AQB, this record drives the nonlinear stress‐strain loop: choice of constitutive law, iteration limits (KMIN/KMAX), line‐search parameters (ALPH, FMAX), and which checks (CHKC/T/S, FAT, SIGS) get performed on elements or sections.

Records marked with an asterisk (*) are primarily design or stiffness‐update controllers and are automatically included when AQB design modules are active. Together, they give the user full control—from raw load definition through higher‐order nonlinear analysis to code‐checking and reinforcement design—within a single, block‐driven input structure.

The table shown is the generic “four-column” input specification that SOFiSTiK uses for any record requiring 

•  a  literal control option (OPT)  
•  one or more associated values (VAL, VAL1, VAL2)  

It can be read as follows:

1.  Column “Item”  
    –  OPT  
       •  The primary keyword or control option for the record.  This is always a literal (LIT).  
    –  VAL  
       •  The first (or only) value associated with the OPT keyword.  Depending on the record, it may be numeric, literal, or a mix (hence “–/LIT”).  
    –  VAL1, VAL2  
       •  Optional additional values.  Used whenever a record needs more than one parameter.  These follow the same input rules as VAL.

2.  Column “Description”  
    –  OPT:  “Control option”  
       •  Here you enter one of the predefined sub-options for that record.  For example, in a CTRL record OPT might be I, II, CABL, TRUS, etc.  
    –  VAL:  “Option value”  
       •  The principal parameter that the chosen sub-option (OPT) acts upon.  In a CTRL record this could be the number of allowed iterations (ITER), group divisor (GDIV), PLF-reference load case (PLC), etc.  
    –  VAL1, VAL2:  “Optional further values”  
       •  When a single VAL is not sufficient—for instance specifying up to six primary load cases for stiffness (PLC VAL1–VAL6)—these fields collect the extra inputs.

3.  Column “Unit”  
    –  “LIT”  
       •  Indicates that the field must be entered as a text token (e.g. KABA, TRUS, CABL).  
    –  “–/LIT”  
       •  Indicates that the field may be either a numeric value or a literal.  Numeric values follow the usual SOFiSTiK conventions (decimal point, no thousands separators).  

4.  Column “Default”  
    –  “–”  
       •  No default: the user must supply OPT explicitly.  
    –  “*”  
       •  Mandatory: at least one of VAL, VAL1 or VAL2 must appear.  There is no system default.

How this table is used in context  
•  Every record type defined in the manual (e.g. CTRL, CHKC, SIGS, TANS, FAT, etc.) will include its own version of this four-column layout, listing exactly which OPT-keywords are allowed and how many VAL-fields are needed.  
•  If you supply an input block that contains loads but no CTRL record, the program interprets it as a “load generation” run (it only reads and stores loads).  
•  If you supply an input block with a CTRL record and loads, it becomes a full “analysis run.”  
•  If you supply a block with CTRL but without loads, it becomes a “restart run,” re-using the last block’s loads.  

Example (CTRL record snippet)  
  CTRL, OPT=TRUS, VAL=IIB, VAL1=3, VAL2=1000  

–  OPT=TRUS tells the solver to allow cable elements in compression (user must later check results).  
–  VAL=IIB selects third-order theory type IIB for beams/trusses.  
–  VAL1=3 requests three iterations.  
–  VAL2=1000 would—for instance—define a custom line-search maximum if that parameter were mapped to VAL2 in the CTRL definition.  

In your RAG-vector store you would index each table entry under its record name (CTRL, CHKS, etc.), then under each OPT, and finally under VAL/VAL1/VAL2 semantics, along with unit and default constraints.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the GRP input table, which defines how element groups are handled in a static or dynamic analysis. This description also draws on the surrounding contextual notes (e.g. default behaviors, interaction with load cases, second-order theory requirements, etc.).

1. Record Purpose  
   • GRP activates one or more “groups” of elements (a group is a subset defined by element number ÷ group-divisor).  
   • Only one GRP selection may appear in a block; if omitted, the previous GRP remains in force.  
   • Within each group, you can override defaults—for prestress, section properties, stiffness, dead load factors, shear-centre treatment, etc.—to control modeling accuracy or drive special-case behavior.

2. Table Fields

Item: NO  
– Description: Group number.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: (none)  
– Notes: Must match the integer group index under which elements were pre-classified.

Item: VAL  
– Description: Activation flag for this group.  
– Unit: Literal (LIT)  
– Default: FULL  
– Allowed Values:  
   • OFF – group is deactivated (elements not used)  
   • YES – group is used, but results are not printed  
   • FULL – group is used and reaction/stress results printed  

Item: STIF  
– Description: Stiffness treatment parameter.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: 1  
– Allowed Values:  
   • 1 – consider rotation of principal axes along member  
   • 0 – do not consider rotation  
   • LIN1 – same as “1” but mark group as not designed (linear only)  
   • LIN0 – same as “0” but linear only, not designed  
– Notes: Some codes require stiffness reduction by material safety factor for second-order analysis; this is a group-level switch.

Item: SECT  
– Description: Choice of cross-section values.  
– Unit: Literal (LIT)  
– Default: * (inherited from previous block or run)  
– Allowed Values:  
   • BRUT – use effective gross cross-section (code-compliant reduced)  
   • TOTA – use total (undegraded) cross-section  
   • DESI – use design section (total ÷ γm material safety factor)  
– Notes: In all cases, the area entry is replaced by the chosen cross-sectional area.

Item: SC  
– Description: Shear-centre effect in beam analysis.  
– Unit: Literal (LIT)  
– Default: FULL  
– Allowed Values:  
   • NONE – ignore shear-centre effects  
   • YES – include shear-centre offset only in applied loads  
   • FULL – fully account for shear-centre in stiffness & loading  

Item: PRES  
– Description: Prestress loading components to consider.  
– Unit: Literal (LIT)  
– Default: FULL  
– Allowed Values:  
   • FULL – include all prestress effects (axial + torsion)  
   • NOTO – suppress torsional prestress components  
   • REST – include only statically indeterminate (redundant) prestress  
   • UNRE – include only statically determinate prestress  
   • URNT – combination of UNRE + NOTO  

Item: FACS  
– Description: Multiplicative factor on linear stiffnesses of this group.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: 1.0  
– Notes: If >1.0 for any load case with factor >1.0, design (reduced) stiffness is used.

Item: FACG  
– Description: Dead-weight scaling factor for this group.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: 1.0  
– Notes: Applies as an additional multiplier to DLX, DLY, DLZ entries in LC records.

Item: CS  
– Description: Construction stage number.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: (none)  
– Notes: Allows stage-wise activation/deactivation of elements.

Item: FACP  
– Description: Factor of prestress.  
– Unit: —  
– Default: 1.0  
– Notes: Scales all prestress loads in the group.

3. Contextual Remarks  
– If FACT is used in an LC record, loads are copied to a new case with that factor; FACS and FACG from GRP apply afterward.  
– For second-order or nonlinear runs (NSTR), stiffness and prestress factors influence convergence and result fidelity.  
– Cross-section selection (SECT) interfaces with code-driven checking (e.g. DIN 18800, Eurocode 2nd order theory).  
– Shear-centre choice (SC) may be critical in deep or unsymmetrical sections.  
– Prestress controls (PRES, FACP) let you simulate partial -values or turn off unwanted components.  
– Only one GRP block per set of load‐cases; if you need different group parameters per case, separate your LC/INFL inputs into distinct blocks.

This grouping mechanism gives fine control over how subsets of elements behave under loads, prestress, staged construction, and code-specific stiffness reductions.

The excerpted input‐table defines the two parameters you must supply when you invoke an Influence-Line load case (INFL) in a STAR2 block. In SOFiSTiK’s terminology this table belongs to the “INFL” record and tells the program which load‐case number will hold the calculated influence line and—optionally—how you want to label it. Below is a guided walkthrough of each column and row, augmented by context from the adjacent documentation:

1. Table Structure  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item: the keyword you type in your input deck (NO or TITL).  
     – Description: a short human-readable summary of what that keyword controls.  
     – Unit: the format or data type you must observe.  
     – Default: the value assumed if you omit this line altogether.  

2. Parameter “NO”  
   – Purpose: designates the load‐case number under which the computed influence line will be stored.  Each INFL record must be associated with a unique, integer load‐case ID.  
   – Valid Range: 1 to 999.  
   – Unit Column: marked with “—” because it is a pure integer index rather than a physical quantity.  
   – Default Behavior: if you do not explicitly specify NO, the program assumes NO = 1.  However, best practice is to assign a load‐case number that does not clash with any existing LC or INFL identifiers in your model.  
   – Contextual Note: This “NO” value is the same kind of identifier you use elsewhere in STAR2’s LC records.  When you later request influence‐line results from the database or plot them, you will reference this number.

3. Parameter “TITL”  
   – Purpose: provides an optional title string (up to 24 characters) for your influence‐line load case.  This is purely for documentation and helps you track what each INFL case represents (e.g. “Moment MY @ Beam-1001 Pos2”).  
   – Unit Column: “LIT24” indicates a literal text field, maximum length 24.  
   – Default Behavior: if omitted, no title is stored (displayed as “–” in the table).  
   – Contextual Note: while TITL has no effect on the numerical computation, it greatly aids post-processing, especially when you generate plots or tables of influence lines via DBVIEW or MAXIMA.  

4. How This Fits Into the INFL Workflow  
   • Before INFL: you must have defined one or more loading patterns via SOFILOAD (using LC, BEPL, STEL, etc.) and captured them under a load‐case number (say 191 or 192).  
   • In the STAR2 input block: you insert  
       INFL 91  
       LCC 191   $ to copy the pre‐defined loads into case 91  
     Here “91” is your NO; you could add a TITL line if you want:  
       TITL “IL_Moment_MY_B1001_P2”  
   • What STAR2 does: it computes only the displacements (i.e. the influence line) along the structure for the requested point of interest and stores results under load‐case 91.  

5. Best Practices and Tips  
   – Always choose a clear, unique NO for each INFL case to prevent overwriting previous results.  
   – Use TITL to document the type of influence line (moment, shear, reaction) and its location—this greatly simplifies later plotting and report generation.  
   – Remember that 2nd‐order effects are not available in an INFL case; if you need geometrically nonlinear influence lines, you must use a nonlinear analysis workaround.  

By strictly following this table’s definitions and integrating it with the SOFILOAD → INFL → LCC workflow, you ensure that your influence‐line cases are correctly numbered, readily identifiable, and seamlessly integrated into SOFiSTiK’s post‐processing environment.

The table is a compact reference showing how to generate the five most common influence lines in a SOFiSTiK‐STAR2 analysis (INFL load case).  Each row links the desired response (“Influence line”) to the kind of unit excitation you must define in SOFiLOAD (“Required loading”) and gives a concrete load‐definition keyword (“e.g.”) you would write in your LC / SOFILOAD block.

1.  Influence line: Moment My  
    • Required loading: Unit rotation about the local y‐axis at the section of interest  
    • SOFILOAD example:  
      BEPL  <element_no>  TYPE DY 1.0  A=<position>  
    Explanation: BEPL TYPE DY applies a unit angular displacement (1 rad) in the element’s local y‐direction.  STAR2 will compute the bending moment My influence line along that beam.

2.  Influence line: Axial force Nx  
    • Required loading: Unit longitudinal displacement  
    • SOFILOAD example:  
      BEPL  <element_no>  TYPE WX 1.0  A=<position>  
    Explanation: BEPL TYPE WX prescribes a unit axial shift (1 mm or user units) so that STAR2 returns the axial‐force influence line.

3.  Influence line: Shear force Vz  
    • Required loading: Unit transverse (z‐direction) displacement  
    • SOFILOAD example:  
      BEPL  <element_no>  TYPE WZ 1.0  A=<position>  
    Explanation: BEPL TYPE WZ enforces a unit lateral displacement at the section, producing the shear‐force influence diagram.

4.  Influence line: Support reaction (forces or moments)  
    • Required loading: Nodal displacement in the reaction’s degree of freedom  
    • SOFILOAD example:  
      NODE  <node_no>  WXX (rotation about X)  
      NODE  <node_no>  WYY (rotation about Y)  
      NODE  <node_no>  WZZ (rotation about Z)  
    Explanation: By “pushing” the support node in the DOF you want the reaction for, STAR2 calculates the reaction influence line.

5.  Influence line: Displacement (global or local)  
    • Required loading: Unit point‐load in the direction of interest  
    • SOFILOAD example:  
      STEL  <grid_or_node> PX (force in global X)  
      STEL  <grid_or_node> PY (force in global Y)  
      STEL  <grid_or_node> PZ (force in global Z)  
    Explanation: STEL applies a concentrated load; STAR2 then prints the displacement influence line at your chosen observation point.

How to use this table:  
– In your SOFILOAD block, start with an LC record (e.g. LC 191).  
– Define the unit‐load pattern following the table (BEPL, NODE or STEL).  
– Close SOFILOAD, then in a STAR2 block issue:  
    INFL <new_loadcase_no>  
    LCC <sofiload_lc_no>   $ copy the pattern  
– Run STAR2; it will compute and print only displacements for that INFL case (no 2nd‐order).

This mapping ensures you always pick the correct unit‐load type to extract bending moments, axial forces, shears, reactions or displacements via influence‐line analysis.

The table under discussion defines the fields available in the “LC” (Load Case) input record of the STAR-analysis environment.  It is arranged in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and lists all parameters you can supply when creating or invoking a load case.  Below is a structured outline, suitable for a RAG-style vector store, capturing each row as an independent semantic entry.  
  
1. Record Overview  
   • Purpose:  Specify or invoke a structural load case for analysis.  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item:  Parameter name (keyword) used on the LC line.  
     – Description:  What the parameter controls.  
     – Unit:  Measurement unit or literal type.  
     – Default:  Value assumed if you omit the parameter.  
  
2. Item = NO  
   • Description:  Load case number (integer from 1 to 999).  
     – Special keyword “ALL” triggers processing of every load case stored in the database.  
   • Unit:  none  
   • Default: 1  
  
3. Item = FACT  
   • Description:  Global multiplier for all loads of type P (forces) and M (moments) in this case.  
     – If FACT > 1.0 then design (“DESI”) stiffnesses from the GRP record are used automatically (per second-order code rules such as DIN 18800).  
     – FACT only affects P/M loads; dead-load factors DLX/DLY/DLZ are unaffected here.  
   • Unit:  none  
   • Default: 1  
  
4. Items = DLX, DLY, DLZ  
   • Description:  Individual load‐factor for the dead weight components in the global x, y, z directions.  
     – Overrides a global FACT factor only for self-weight loads imported from SOFiLOAD.  
     – If omitted, DLX = DLY = DLZ = 0 → no dead loads unless explicitly re-activated by SOFiLOAD.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 0  
  
5. Item = TITL  
   • Description:  Alphanumeric title (up to 24 characters) for the load case.  
   • Unit: LIT24 (24-character literal)  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
  
6. Item = TYPE  
   • Description:  Action or load category designation.  
     – Exposes the case to later superposition or combination in MAXIMA.  
     – Matches TYPE literals defined in the SOFiLOAD ACT record (e.g. ‘PROP’, ‘TEMP’, ‘WIND’, etc.).  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
  
7. Items = GAMU, GAMF, GAMA  
   • GAMU: Unfavourable safety factor (γ<sub>U</sub>)  
   • GAMF: Favourable safety factor (γ<sub>F</sub>)  
   • GAMA: Accidental safety factor (γ<sub>A</sub>)  
   • Usage:  Overrides default partial factors for the given action type during later combination.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: “*” (inherit from TYPE or from SOFiLOAD if not explicitly set)  
  
8. Items = PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S  
   • Description: Combination coefficients Ψ<sub>0</sub> (rare), Ψ<sub>1</sub> (frequent), Ψ<sub>2</sub> (quasi-permanent), Ψ<sub>1S</sub> (non-frequent).  
   • Role:  Specify reduction factors for accompanying variable loads in ultimate and serviceability limit-state combinations.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: “*” (use code-defined defaults unless overridden)  
  
9. Items = CRI1, CRI2, CRI3  
   • Description: User‐defined criteria fields I, II and III.  
     – Free-field numeric tags for post-processing (e.g. store results thresholds, custom check flags).  
     – TALPA uses CRI1 to carry a material safety factor in Fellenius slip‐circle stability analyses if needed.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: 0  
  
10. Interactions & Special Notes  
    – If LC is followed by no load definitions, all previously defined loads (including DW) are simply scaled by FACT and re-imported.  
    – If you specify any new loads after LC, old loads for that case number are purged first.  
    – To compute influence lines instead of standard load‐case results, one uses INFL instead of LC (see “INFL – Definition of an Influence Line Load Case”).  
    – Only one LC or INFL record per analysis block is allowed; omitting both retains the prior case selection.  
  
Summary  
The LC record table provides full control over which load case to run (NO/ALL), how to scale its loads (FACT, DLX/DLY/DLZ), how to identify it (TITL, TYPE) and how to set safety-factor and combination-coefficient metadata (GAMU, GAMF, GAMA, PSI*, CRI*). These parameters drive both the structural solver and any subsequent combination or postprocessing tools (MAXIMA, DBVIEW, TALPA).

The table defines the set of input‐data fields you must supply when you want to pick up previously computed element or nodal loads (for example, when using the LCC or LV command in STAAD‐type pre/post processors).  Its four columns are:

  • Item  
    – the keyword you type in your input file  
  • Description  
    – a short explanation of what that keyword controls  
  • Unit  
    – the physical unit (in this case “–” means “dimensionless” or “not applicable”)  
  • Default  
    – the value that will be assumed if you omit that keyword  

Below is a breakdown of each row:

1. NO  
   • Description: “Number of a load case up to max. 999.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: – (mandatory field; no default)

   You must supply the load‐case number whose loads you want to import or multiply (for LCC) or whose results you want to convert into loads (for LV).

2. FACT  
   • Description: “Factor for load values.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1

   A scalar multiplier applied to all imported loads.  For example, FACT = –1 will subtract previously applied loads; FACT > 1 amplifies them.

3. FROM, TO, INC  
   • Description: “Range data for beam numbers.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Defaults:  
     – TO defaults to the same value as FROM  
     – INC defaults to 1  

   Use this triplet to define a contiguous list of beam elements whose loads/results you wish to import.  If you specify only FROM = a, then TO = a and INC = 1 are assumed (i.e. a single beam).

4. NFRO, NTO, NINC  
   • Description: “Range data for node numbers.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Defaults:  
     – NTO → NFRO  
     – NINC → 1  

   Analogous to FROM/TO/INC but for nodal loads.  Defaults pick only the single node NFRO if you omit NTO and NINC.

5. TFRO, TTO, TINC  
   • Description: “Range data for truss‐bar numbers.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Defaults:  
     – TTO → TFRO  
     – TINC → 1  

   Same pattern, now applied to truss‐bar elements.

6. CFRO, CTO, CINC  
   • Description: “Range data for cable numbers.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Defaults:  
     – CTO → CFRO  
     – CINC → 1  

   Follows the same logic for cable‐element ranges.

How it all ties together:  

• At the simplest, you must always supply NO (the load case you want to draw from) and optionally FACT if you need to scale those loads.  
• If you do nothing else, all beams/trusses/cables/nodes defined in that load‐case will be picked up.  
• If, however, you give FROM/TO/INC etc., you restrict the import to just those element or node ID ranges.  
• Negative FACT allows you to subtract out previously applied initial deformations (e.g. to remove old “imperfections” before re‐applying them with a different factor).  
• The fact that all “Unit” entries are blank tells you these fields are purely identifiers or scalars, not physical quantities like kN or m.  

In practice you might see input blocks such as:

  NO  12  
  FACT  –1.0  
  FROM  100  TO 200  INC 5

…which would take the results from load‐case 12 for beams 100, 105, 110, …, 200, multiply them by –1, and add them into your current analysis step.

The table shown defines the keyword‐card inputs for STAR2’s “LV” (Load from Results) or “LCC” (Load Case Combination) records.  It tells the solver which previously computed load case to pull results from, how to manipulate them (creep, shrinkage, initial‐deformation factors), which elements to affect, and how to treat construction‐stage or prestress loads.  Below is a row‐by‐row breakdown of each field, its meaning, units and default.  

1.  NO  
   • Description: Identifier of an existing STAR2 load case to be re‐used (up to 999).  
   • Unit: – (integer index)  
   • Default: none (must be specified)  
   • Notes: Under LCC this load case’s entire load set is scaled by FACT and added to the current one; under LV it is the source of beam/truss/cable result extraction.

2.  PHI  
   • Description: Creep‐adjustment factor for strains or curvatures.  PHI multiplies internal forces (normal N, bending MZ, MY) to generate additional “creep” curvature loads via  
        K1 = PHI;  
        K2 = PHI·MZ/EIZ or MY/EIY  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes: Typical creep of statically determinate cases uses PHI = ϕ; negative PHI (–1.0) can subtract previous deformations.

3.  EPS  
   • Description: Shrinkage (axial‐strain) coefficient.  Acts in tandem with PHI to produce total strain load ES = EPS + PHI·N/EF.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless strain)  
   • Default: 0.0  

4.  FACV  
   • Description: Factor for importing stored elastic deflections as an affine initial deformation.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes:  FACV·(elastic line) defines initial imperfection/buckling modes.  To remove old imperfections one can issue LCC with FACT = –1.

5.  FROM  
   • Description: Start of element (beam/truss/cable) number range whose results will be imported.  
   • Unit: – (integer index)  
   • Default: 1 (when no FROM is given, all elements in the source case are included)  

6.  TO  
   • Description: End of the element‐number range.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: same as FROM  

7.  INC  
   • Description: Increment for stepping through element numbers between FROM and TO.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1  

8.  STIF  
   • Description: Load‐case index whose element stiffnesses are used to convert forces into deformations (if omitted, uses stiffnesses of NO).  
   • Unit: – (integer index)  
   • Default: NO  

9.  CSMI  
   • Description: Lowest construction‐stage index to include.  Used when extracting loads or deformations associated with intermediate erection phases.  
   • Unit: – (integer index)  
   • Default: none (all stages)  

10. CSMA  
   • Description: Highest construction‐stage index to include.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: CSMI  

11. K TYP  
   • Description: Type of prestress‐load variation function.  Defines shape functions along each element’s length.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: SPL  
   • Options:  
     – SPL  : cubic variation  
     – POL  : polygonal (piecewise‐linear)  
     – SPL1 : cubic without generating secondary bending components  
     – POL1 : polygonal without secondary bending components  

Additional Context from LV/LCC Functionality  
• LCC (Load Case Combination) multiplies all existing loads from the specified NO by a FACTOR and adds them to the current case (dead weights excluded).  A single NO & FACT input suffices for all elements or nodes.  
• LV (Load from Results) reads beam/truss/cable output from NO, applies creep (PHI), shrinkage (EPS), and initial‐deformation (FACV) factors, and reimposes them as loads in a new step.  It enables modeling of creep effects, construction‐stage constraints, system imperfections (buckling), and prestress‐sequence loading.  

By indexing which elements (FROM, TO, INC) and which construction stages (CSMI, CSMA) to include, plus selecting appropriate K TYP for prestress shape, the user gains fine‐grained control over regeneration and combination of structural loads.

The drawing is a schematic of a three-span continuous beam together with four different “envelope” plots showing how the software can distribute reinforcement according to four control levels—SECT, BEAM, SPAN and GLOB. The single line at the very top represents the beam axis, supported by four simple supports: at the left end, two interior supports beneath span 1 and span 2, and the right-hand pin at the end of span 3. The three spans are numbered “①”, “②” and “③” above the beam line. In the third span the beam depth steps up in the middle (a thicker flange portion) before returning to the original depth at the far support.

Beneath that schematic is a horizontal axis divided into three bracketed regions: “SECT1” covering spans 1+2, “Sect.2” under the deeper middle portion of span 3, and then “SEC” for the remaining part of span 3. The bracket lines indicate that different cross‐section definitions (section numbers) apply over those parts of the beam.

Below the axis are four rows of diagrams, each labeled on the left:

1. SECT  
   A solid “histogram” fill (vertical bar‐shaded outline) shows the minimum reinforcement per cross section. Within each section region the bars vary up and down as the code computes the minimum steel area required by code or by a database, stepping abruptly at section boundaries. This plot reflects purely local, section‐by‐section minima (AM1–AM4 in EN 1992).

2. BEAM  
   A dashed‐line curve illustrating the reinforcement that results when a BEAM record is used. The curve follows the general shape of the SECT minima but superposes the global minimum over each individual section, producing a smooth envelope that cannot go below the BEAM‐specified reinforcement level. Where the beam depth increases in span 3, the dashed curve jumps upward, then drops back.

3. SPAN  
   Another dashed curve similar in style but now flat within each span. In each of the three span regions the plot is essentially the interpolation of the peak required reinforcement for that entire span (multiplied by the safety factor). At each span boundary the curve steps to the next span’s level. This corresponds to the SPAN record: the same section number repeated across an entire span uses the maximum reinforcement from that repeated group.

4. GLOB  
   A final dashed curve that is constant or gently varying across the whole beam, reflecting the global minimum reinforcement for all connected ranges with the same section number. Here the envelope is the maximum of all sectional maxima times the global safety factor, so none of the local dips in SECT or BEAM can fall below this GLOB‐defined baseline. Again, jumps occur at section transitions.

At the bottom is the figure caption:  
Figure 3.1: Distribution of reinforcements  

Taken together, the four plots demonstrate how AQUA/AQB allow the user to control whether reinforcement is governed purely by each cross section’s minimum (SECT), by a beam‐wide minimum (BEAM), by the maximum required within each span (SPAN), or by a single global minimum (GLOB). They also illustrate the effect of superposition: local minima are never allowed to drop below the higher‐level minima imposed by BEAM, SPAN or GLOB records.

The little four-column table at the end of your excerpt is a concise summary of three post-processing “P‐parameters” (P9, P10 and P11) used by AQB/AQUA during reinforced‐concrete section design.  In a RAG/vector‐store context it can be broken down as follows:

1. Column-by-column breakdown  
   • Parameter Code (P#)  
   • Description of what the parameter controls  
   • The hard‐coded “Default” value used by the program when the user does not override it  
   • The “Typical” range or recommended setting that a designer might choose for fine-tuning  

2. Row-by-row interpretation  

   a) P9 – Factor for reference point of strain  
      • Description: P9 scales the zero‐ or reference‐strain location in the section.  In multidimensional (biaxial) bending this moves the assumed neutral axis so as to adjust the relative weight of compression versus tension.  
      • Default: 1.0 (neutral axis at the geometric centroid, no shift)  
      • Typical: 1.0 (almost always left at the default, unless an advanced user needs to offset the neutral axis to reflect unsymmetrical boundary conditions or pre-compression effects)  

   b) P10 – Factor for reference point of moments  
      • Description: P10 scales the zero‐moment reference location.  It effectively weights the bending‐moment residuals in the BFGS or least‐squares iteration (see the error function MN in the text).  A lower P10 shifts the solver’s emphasis toward reducing the moment error rather than the axial‐force or strain errors.  
      • Default: 1.0 (equal weighting between tensile and bending moment errors)  
      • Typical: 0.2 – 1.0 (users often reduce P10 below 1.0 in sections with extreme biaxial bending to improve convergence by de-emphasizing the moment terms)  

   c) P11 – Factor for preference of outer reinforcement  
      • Description: P11 caps how much of the total outer (extreme fiber) reinforcement may be occupied by a single layer or grouping.  By code (e.g. EN 1992, DIN 1045) you cannot place more than one‐third of the lever arm’s reinforcement in one thin layer, and P11 scales that fraction for uniaxial vs. biaxial cases.  
      • Default: “*” (the program chooses P11 internally based on loading type: P11 = 1.0 for biaxial bending or when the detailed lever arm check is enforced; P11 = 0.0 for pure uniaxial bending, effectively disabling the one‐third rule)  
      • Typical: 0.0 – 1.0 (explicitly set between 0 and 1 if the user wants to control how much outer reinforcement is driven to the extreme fiber; e.g., setting P11 = 0.5 limits any single layer to no more than 50 % of the allowable max in that position)  

3. Contextual linkage to the broader AQUA/AQB design process  
   • P9 and P10 enter the objective‐function weighting (alongside P7 and P8) when the program iterates inner‐loop strain planes using the BFGS method.  Poor convergence under biaxial loading is often cured by adjusting P7, P8, P9 or P10 so that the design problem remains convex.  
   • P11 ties into the code checks on lever arm and ductility.  If the computed steel strain at the outer fiber does not exceed the prescribed S1 value (ductility requirement), P11 can be used to force a minimum compressive reinforcement and shear links per EN 1992 or DIN 1045.  
   • These P-parameters are normally buried behind higher-level AQUA/INI settings (e.g. minimum reinforcement AM1–AM4, safety factors SC1–SS0, tendon groups ZGRP), but are available for expert users to fine-tune convergence and minimum‐lever‐arm rules without rewriting the section geometry or reinforcement layout records.  

4. How to store/retrieve for RAG  
   • Index by the parameter code (P9, P10, P11).  
   • Store attributes: “description,” “default_value,” “typical_range,” “notes_on_usage.”  
   • Link back to the broader “reinforcement design” document chunk that defines P7, P8, strain‐plane iteration, code-specific lever‐arm limits, and convergence strategies.  

This descriptive entry will allow a retrieval‐augmented generator to answer questions such as “What does P10 control in AQUA’s section design?”, “When should I reduce P10 below 1.0?”, or “How does P11 interact with EN 1992 ductility checks?” with immediate access to both the numeric defaults and design rationale.

The table shown is part of the input‐record definitions for AQB/AQUA’s reinforced‐concrete bending and shear design.  It defines a small set of parameters governing shear‐force checks, strut inclinations, plasticity limits and ductile redistribution.  The four columns are “Item” (the keyword), “Description” (what the parameter controls), “Unit,” and “Default.”  Below is a structured description of each row and its sub-options:

1.  SMOD  
    ·  Description: Design mode for shear checks  
    ·  Unit: LIT (a literal keyword)  
    ·  Default: “*” (i.e. inherited or unspecified)  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  If SMOD = NO, no shear‐reinforcement design is performed; internal shear stresses are neither checked nor calculated.  

2.  TVS  
    ·  Description: Deductional shear stress (sometimes called shear‐stress limit)  
    ·  Unit: N/mm²  
    ·  Default: “*”  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  This value is subtracted from the factored shear stress before computing required shear reinforcement.  

3.  MSCD  
    ·  Description: Maximum permissible tensile longitudinal stress in bending members  
    ·  Unit: N/mm²  
    ·  Default: “*”  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  If the computed normal stress in the section exceeds MSCD, shear capacity is reduced accordingly.  

4.  KTAU  
    ·  Description: Plate‐shear design variant  
    ·  Unit: –/LIT (literal choices or numeric coefficient)  
    ·  Default: “*”  
    ·  Sub-options:  
       •  K1    : non-staggered punching shear for regular (one-way) slabs (per DIN 1045 17.5.5 eq. 14)  
       •  K2    : non-staggered punching shear for slabs with uniform distributed loads (DIN 1045 17.5.5 eq. 15)  
       •  K1S   : same as K1 but with staggered shear per table 13 1a of DIN 1045 17.5.5  
       •  K2S   : same as K2 but with staggered shear arrangement  
       •  num   : a user‐supplied coefficient k as in EC2 eq. 4.18 (e.g. 0.4, 0.6)  
       •  0.0   : deactivates the plate shear check entirely  

5.  TTOL  
    ·  Description: Tolerance applied to limit‐state inequality checks (e.g. for shear, bending)  
    ·  Unit: dimensionless  
    ·  Default: 0.02  

6.  TANA  
    ·  Description: Lower/upper limits for the inclination (tangent of angle) of shear‐resisting struts in the truss model  
    ·  Unit: –  
    ·  Default: “*”  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  Should now be specified via the TVAR record rather than directly here.  

7.  TANB  
    ·  Description: Alternate notation for strut‐inclination limits (deprecated)  
    ·  Unit: –  
    ·  Default: “*”  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  Superseded by TVAR; maintained only for backward compatibility.  

8.  SCL  
    ·  Description: Plasticity control for steel and composite sections under bending  
    ·  Unit: –  
    ·  Default: 3  
    ·  Options:  
       1.  No limits on steel strain (fully elastic–plastic)  
       2.  Limit only the outermost compressive‐steel yield strain  
       3.  Limit compressive steel strain to the yield value (default)  
       4.  Enforce yield‐strain limit in both tensile and compressive reinforcement  

9.  DELR  
    ·  Description: Redistribution limit for ductile sections, defined as x/D (neutral‐axis depth over effective depth)  
    ·  Unit: –  
    ·  Default: 1.0  
    ·  Notes:  
       –  Controls the maximum allowable moment redistribution in continuous or statically indeterminate members; negative values disable it.  

Summary of table purpose:  
•  Together, these parameters allow the user to tailor the shear‐design procedure (activate or skip it, set stress deductions, choose plate‐punching formulas or EC-2 coefficients), impose numerical tolerances, control allowable strut inclinations in the shear‐truss model, limit steel‐strain exploitation, and cap moment redistributions in ductile members.  
•  Default values (wildcards “*” or common presets 0.02, 3, 1.0) usually pick up code‐default behavior; non-default settings are only required for special design codes, advanced punching checks or when troubleshooting convergence.

The table defines a series of global control-and-check parameters used when performing stiffness‐and‐stress evaluation (for example in the NSTR crack/non-linear module, or in subsequent STAR2/ASE or DYNA runs) as well as crack‐width and decompression checks.  It is organized into four columns—“Item,” “Description,” “Unit,” and “Default”—and can be cross-referenced with the REIN and DESI definitions that establish load conditions and safety factors.

1. KMOD (–, Default “ ! ”)  
   • Selects the overall load condition and governs whether stiffness is updated:  
     – SERV: stress evaluation without stiffness change  
     – ULTI: ultimate‐state (no stiffness change)  
     – ACCI: accidental load case (no stiffness change)  
     – NONL: non-linear option (see notes for iterative stiffness strategies)  

2. KSV, KSB (–, Default “ * ”)  
   • Control material stiffness of the cross section (KSV) and of reinforcements/tension-stiffening (KSB). “*” means inherit defaults from the chosen load condition (see DESI/NSTR).

3. KMIN, KMAX, ALPH, FMAX (–, Defaults 0.01, 4.00, 0.4, 5.0)  
   • KMIN/KMAX: bounds on the computed element stiffness (secant or tangent)  
   • ALPH: numerical damping factor for iteration stability  
   • FMAX: numerical acceleration factor for convergence  

4. CRAC (LIT, Default “NO”)  
   • Crack/decompression design mode:  
     – NO: no crack check  
     – YES: compute crack widths  
     – TAB: limit steel stress in cracked section  
     – DECO: compute decompression zone around tendons  

5. CW [mm]₁₀₂₆, BB (–, Default “ * ”)  
   • CW: crack width or decompression‐height parameter (mm)  
   • BB: duration/coefficient parameter (e.g. kₜ per EN 1992-1-1, βₜ per DIN 1045-1, tension-stiffening stress per BS, Snip φ₁, Spanish EHE k₂). Default “*” inherits from standards or load case.

6. HMIN, HMAX [mm]₁₀₂₄/₁₀₁₁ (Defaults 0.0, 800)

7. CW-FFCT (–, Default “–”)  
   • Factor applied on the mean tensile strength of concrete  

8. CHKC, CHKT, CHKR (–/MPa, Default “–”)  
   • Strain or stress limits to be checked in concrete (CHKC), tendons (CHKT), and reinforcement (CHKR). Violations are flagged but not automatically remedied due to nonlinear dependencies.

Notes on non-linear stiffness iteration (for KMOD = NONL):  
– S1, SN: secant stiffness from curvature or moment  
– T0, T1, TN: tangent stiffness variants  
– K0, K1, KN: plastic‐strain based stiffness updates

The fragment shown defines two complementary “check strategies” for reinforced‐concrete sections, along with the key parameters and defaults that govern their behavior.  In essence, it’s a lookup table that tells the analysis engine (and ultimately the user) which type of stress‐and‐strain evaluation to perform, what outputs will be generated, and how material safety factors and iteration schemes are selected.

1. Table Overview  
   • Columns  
     – Option name (e.g. NSTR, CHKS)  
     – Description of action performed  
     – Quantity being checked (“Strain/stress to be checked for structural steel”)  
     – Units (–/MPa)  
     – Placeholder for additional flags or modifiers (“–”)  
   • See also references: REIN (reinforcement description) and DESI (design definitions).

2. Row 1: NSTR (“Nonlinear STRess/strain evaluation”)  
   • Performs a full nonlinear analysis of cracked and uncracked behavior.  
   • Carries out checks in the cracked state or other nonlinear regimes.  
   • “Byproducts” generated:  
     – Stress ranges in the steel  
     – Crack widths in the concrete  
     – Nonlinear (secant or tangent) stiffness parameters  
   • These results feed forward into subsequent dynamic or advanced‐serviceability modules (STAR2, ASE, DYNA).

3. Row 2: CHKS (“CHecK Stresses”)  
   • Executes stress checks on concrete sections or on reinforcement only.  
   • Violations of preset stress limits are flagged, but no corrective iterations or reinforcement updates are triggered.  
   • Rationale: nonlinear couplings between steel and concrete make automatic “fixes” impractical within a simple check routine.

4. Load-Condition Definitions & Defaults  
   • The choice of material strengths and safety factors is controlled by a “load condition” code.  If DESI (design input) and NSTR uniquely specify a condition, default safety factors are implied for concrete (KSB) and steel (KSV).  They may be overridden manually.  
   • Standard load conditions:  
     – EL: linear elastic (no concrete tension)  
     – ELD: as EL, but with material safety factors  
     – SL: serviceability, nominal  
     – SLD: serviceability, design  
     – UL: ultimate limit state, nominal  
     – ULD: ultimate limit state, design  
     – CAL: calculatoric mean values  
     – AQUA: CAL with AQUA‐defined safeties  
   • Default pairings (unless overridden):  
     – Serviceability → KSV=KSB=SL  
     – Ultimate limit state → read from INI file (often KSV=SLD, KSB=SL)  
     – Accidental (ACCI) → KSV=KSB=SL  
     – Nonlinear (NONL) → KSV=KSB=CAL

5. Iterative Stiffness Schemes  
   • When NSTR (or NONL) is selected, you choose how to update stiffness at each iteration:  
     – Secant based on curvature: S1  
     – Secant based on bending moment: SN  
     – Plastic strains without iteration: K0  
     – Plastic strains from curvature: K1  
     – Plastic strains from moment: KN  
   • Alternatively, tangent‐stiffness approaches:  
     – T0: no iteration  
     – T1: from curvature  
     – TN: from moment  
   • The complete code for a nonlinear serviceability analysis using curvature‐based secant stiffness would be “NS1.”  

6. Tension-Stiffening Adjustment  
   • To capture post‐cracking tension capacity, the steel‐concrete stress–strain laws are modified:  
     – Either by prescribing an effective reinforcement ratio in the steel material definition  
     – Or by applying residual tensile stress in the cracked concrete  

This structured description ensures that anyone indexing this table for a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store will know exactly which flags are set, what checks are performed under each option, and how the load‐condition codes and iteration strategies interplay in the nonlinear analysis framework.

Calculation of non-linear stiffnesses in AQB with other values than S0 is successful only if another program like ASE, STAR2 or DYNA is called again with a new iteration as a restart, and this process is repeated until convergence occurs. Thus it is recommended to define these records within ASE or STAR2 and to define the number of iterations there. Within the procedure WPS/SPS it is possible to call several programs in turn with the option PROG ITER which is optimized however for the use with STAR2 (cf. AQB 5.2.2. prefabricated column).
 An analysis of unloading or the hysteresis of load cycles is not possible today for beam ele- ments!
 Selection of the optimum iteration method is not easy, because the selected type of stiffness update determines the iteration and convergence behaviour. In most cases the use of KMOD S1 or SN will be straight forward. KMOD SN is the fastest method for slightly nonlinear prob- lems, while S1 is suited for highly loaded systems where it may happen that the ultimate load capacity of a section is exceeded within an iteration step. For the methods K0, K1 or KN the stiffness will be kept constant, but plastic strains are calculated, to be used as extra loading as initial strains similar to a temperature loading. Using this approach the failure of the system is no longer given by an instability detected during the solution of the equation system, but by monotone increasing deformations, which have to be checked carefully therefore.
 The user should start with SN for lightly loaded systems and with S1 for more heavily loaded systems, and should then shift to K1 or K0 if necessary. When there are many similar systems, it pays to find the optimum method by experimentation.

The table shown is the definition of the ECHO-command’s input syntax in AQB/AQUA. ECHO is used to turn on or off various groups of printed output (node coordinates, internal forces, reinforcement details, etc.) and to select how much detail is produced. The command takes two fields, OPT and VAL, each of type literal (LIT), and each has its own default. Below is a detailed walk-through of each column and the values it may assume.

1. Item “OPT”  
   – Purpose: Specifies which category (or “option”) of results you want to control.  
   – Type (Unit): LIT (a literal string keyword).  
   – Default: FULL  
   – Allowed Literals:  
     • NODE   – prints node coordinates and support constraints  
     • BEAM   – prints beam element geometry and connectivity  
     • SPRI   – prints spring‐element definitions  
     • BOUN   – prints distributed support elements  
     • SECT   – prints cross‐sectional properties (as defined in AQUA)  
     • MAT    – prints material constants (as defined in AQUA)  
     • LOAD   – prints applied loads  
     • FORC   – prints internal forces and moments  
     • DEFO   – prints beam deformations  
     • BDEF   – prints nodal displacements (boundary-defined displacements)  
     • REAC   – prints support reactions  
     • REIN   – prints reinforcement layouts and areas  
     • NSTR   – prints strains and stiffnesses  
     • STEP   – prints every iteration in a nonlinear analysis  
     • FULL   – a shorthand that turns on ALL of the above  

   By default (if you do not supply an ECHO card), AQB will suppress some categories (NODE, BEAM, SPRI, BOUN, SECT, MAT, BDEF), set FORC to FULL, and enable the rest (DEFO, REAC, REIN, NSTR, STEP) at YES level.

2. Item “VAL”  
   – Purpose: Defines the verbosity level for the chosen OPT.  
   – Type (Unit): LIT  
   – Default: FULL  
   – Allowed Literals:  
     • NO    – do not print this category at all  
     • YES   – print at the standard (moderate) level of detail  
     • FULL  – print all available detail for this category  
     • EXTR  – print the maximum, “extreme” level of detail  

   In practice you would combine OPT and VAL in one or more ECHO cards. Examples:  
     • ECHO NODE YES        – include node coordinates at standard detail  
     • ECHO FORC FULL       – include all internal forces and moments  
     • ECHO NSTR EXTR       – include every strain and stiffness output in an “extreme” listing  
     • ECHO STEP NO         – suppress printing of intermediate nonlinear‐analysis steps

It gets checked by every iteration step, whether the accuracy lies within the prescribed limits. This is performed separately for forces, moments, displacements and rotations. The procedure is the following:
 The difference between the result value during the current and the one during the pre- vious iteration is determined at each result point. This difference must be smaller than the absolute result value multiplied by the precision tolerance. If the value is smaller than the largest value encountered in the structure times the precision tolerance, the percentage difference is not computed. This way very small values, which e.g. oscil-
 late around zero from one iteration to the other, thus generating very high percentage changes, get no consideration at all.
 A summary of these values is printed at the beginning of each output iteration. These values are also output to the screen or to the protocol file for all iterations.
